look_here_first: Start with the broad, fleshy, toothed leaves and terminal spine. Compare mature leaf width and the flowering architecture: a branched panicle supports A. americana, while lechuguilla has narrower leaves and a largely spike-like flowering axis.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Broad fleshy rosette leaves, typically (80–)100–200 cm long in the existing FNA-based review.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Marginal teeth about 5–10 mm; a strong terminal spine.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Flowering axis branches into a panicle, unlike the largely spicate lechuguilla axis.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Mature broad succulent leaves; tooth and terminal spine characters should be inspected at close range with scale.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Branched flowering panicle; full flowering-axis photo still needed.

key_traits.label: Lookalike separators
key_traits.text: A. lechuguilla: much narrower leaves, typically 30–50 × 2–4(–5.2) cm, and largely spicate inflorescence. Do not diagnose species or local nativity by blue color, variegation, or ornamental occurrence. Other cultivated agaves can overlap; require reproductive/leaf-edge evidence when uncertain.
